opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
“Denounce him! Let us denounce him!” You can feel the pressure closing in on Jeremiah.  He is in distress, surrounded by people watching him, waiting for him to fall. And then the psalm answers that feeling exactly: “In my distress I called upon the Lord, and he heard my voice.” So already there is this movement from being surrounded by enemies to crying out to God with confidence that He hears.
Then in the Gospel, Jesus is also surrounded, but in a different way. They are pressing Him, accusing Him, trying to trap Him in His own words. But Jesus answers them in their own language, through their own law. He says, if Scripture itself calls them “gods” to whom the word of God came, then why are you calling it blasphemy when I say I am the Son of God?  He is showing them that even in their own Scriptures, those who received God’s word and authority were spoken of in an elevated way, so how can they accuse Him, the one consecrated and sent by the Father, for speaking the truth about who He is?
That is what is so forceful about His words. He does not just argue back. He brings them into a bigger circle. He uses their own law, then lifts it higher, back to the Father, back to the works He is doing, back to the truth that He is not acting on His own at all. He is doing the works of the one who sent Him. Almost like He is saying: even if you struggle with my words, look at what I do. Look at what is right in front of you.
And that is where Jeremiah starts to sound almost like a foreshadowing. “Denounce him!” It has the sound of what Christ Himself will face. Jeremiah is suffering because he bears the word of God. Jesus will suffer not only because He speaks God’s word, but because He is the Word standing in front of them, and still, they do not want to receive Him.
Back then, they were living it in real time. They did not have the whole timeline the way we do. Some believed because they heard. Some believed because they saw. Some were searching, waiting, hoping for the Messiah. He would come, but some refused, even with Him right there in front of them.
And in a way that still has not changed. Today, we can look back and see the pattern, the promise, the fulfillment. We know the history. We know who Christ is. And still some refuse to believe, not because there is no light, but because they choose not to receive it.
And maybe where this meets us personally is this: the Lord hears your voice in distress, yes, but not only in distress. He knows your thoughts before you speak. He knows the heart that is trying to understand Him. He knows the one who is searching, the one who is afraid, the one who believes, and the one who is still struggling to believe. He knows every last hair on your head. The point is that Christ is showing them, and showing us, who He really is. Not just a teacher. Not just a prophet. But the Son of God, sent by the Father, doing the Father’s works, and worthy of belief.
